title: Chapter 123 – The Door in the Soul
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The fourteenth morning.

They come down the stair in single file, and the Dock has never been so crowded.

Yue goes first, with the gray ledger under her arm and Pebble on her shoulder. Ye follows, supporting her teacher with one hand and her stick with the other. Sang Ruo walks. She has said she will, and she does, slowly, her thin bare feet finding each step, her breath whistling in her chest. Behind them Jian carries the lamp. It is the only light on the stair. The register has dimmed itself, out of courtesy, and the walls are the color of old milk.

At the bottom Sang Ruo stops.

She stands at the threshold of the Dock in her gray blanket, and looks at it. The long metal table. The bench. The pale blue bowl, empty now, on its shelf. The Reservoir below, glowing faintly under its dome. She looks at all of it for a long time, with her head a little bent and her pale eyes moving very slowly, as one reads a page in a language one has studied for half a century and never heard spoken.

"So small," she says.

Nobody answers.

"I thought it would be larger." The thin voice is wondering. "Fifty-five years. A thousand sleepers. I thought it would be a hall." She lays one hand flat against the cold wall beside the door. "It is only a room. A quiet room. With a bench in it."

"It is a good room," says Jian.

"I am sure." Her mouth moves. "I only wish it had been kinder to the people who fed it."

She lowers herself into the stone chair, with Ye's arm under her elbow, and does not speak again for some time.

Ye catches his sleeve beside the bench, before he lies down.

She has not slept; he can see it in the thin dry skin under her eyes. She stands with her stick planted and her free hand knotted in the sleeve of her teacher's blanket, and she speaks quietly, so that the old woman, across the room in the stone chair, will not hear.

"I have not said it," she says. "I do not know how."

"You need not."

"I do." Her jaw is hard. "Fifty-five years I told myself she was dead. It was easier. There was a grave in my head, and I put flowers on it every spring." She draws a breath. "She is alive. She is a very old, tired woman who has been dying all her life. And she chose to carry something so that I would not have to. I did not know it. I was angry for half a century at someone who had been carrying me."

Jian says nothing.

"If it goes badly," says Ye. "If you do not come back."

"I will come back."

"If you do not. I will take her up the stair and I will see that she dies in a bed, in the sun, with her pupil beside her." The pale eyes meet his. "And I will see that your family is kept. Whatever the House says. You may put that in your pocket."

He bows. It is the deepest bow he has ever made to anyone but Qin Hao.

* * *

He lies down on the bench, and the cold of it goes through his cloak.

It is a plain gray slab, long enough for a man, with a shallow hollow at the head. He has lain on it eleven times. He knows its chill, and the faint hum of the metal, and the way the lamp swings a little above his face as the register wakes. What he does not know is how it will feel with four people watching and a small animal sitting on his chest.

"Hold my hand," he says.

Yue takes his left. She does not say anything. Her fingers are cool and dry and very strong, and she grips him as one grips a rope over a ravine. Pebble climbs down his sleeve and settles between them, a small warm weight.

I am here, she says.

"I know."

If it goes wrong I will bite.

"Where?"

Wherever is closest.

He laughs. It comes out unsteady. Then he lifts his eyes to the dome, and says in a clear voice, "Open the door."

The register wakes.

He reads it. His heart is going very hard in his chest.

The reader chooses nothing.

"Confirm," he says.

* * *

It is not like the Purple Mansion. There is no silence, no falling. There is only the bench beneath him, and then the bench is not beneath him, and he is standing on a floor that is not there, in a place that has no walls.

It is white.

White floor. White ceiling. White light with no source. The air smells of nothing. In the middle of the emptiness there is a single door, plain and brown, scarred with age, with a lamp burning beside it. It stands ajar. Over the lintel, in letters he knows, someone has carved a name.

COLE, ETHAN.

He crosses the white floor and stops in front of it.

Behind him, very faint, as if heard through water, he can hear Yue's voice saying his name. He does not turn. He lays his palm flat on the old brown wood, and it is warm, as a living thing is warm, and he pushes.

It opens inward without a sound.

The room on the other side is small, and plain, and utterly ordinary.

It is a study. There is a desk against one wall, pale and scuffed, with a lamp on it and a stack of lined paper. There is a chair, a cheap swivel thing with a split in the seat. There is a window with the blinds half drawn, and beyond the blinds a gray morning of low cloud. There is a cup of cold coffee at the elbow of the desk, with a ring on the wood beneath it. And in the chair, with his back to the door, sits a man in a rumpled work shirt, writing.

He does not turn. He does not stop writing. His head is bent, and the pen in his hand is a cheap blue plastic one, chewed at the cap.

"Sit down," he says. His voice is flat and quiet and tired. "It's the chair by the shelf. I'm almost done."

Jian sits.

* * *

"This is a recording," says the man at the desk. "I want to be honest about that. I'm not really here. I made this room in the last week before I went in, when I knew I wouldn't remember what I was about to do, and I filled it with everything I thought a stranger would need. It isn't much. I'm sorry. I'm not a writer."

He lays down the pen. He turns the chair.

He is perhaps thirty-five. Thin, unshaven, with a long pale face and shadows under his eyes. His hair is brown and needs cutting. He wears no ring. There is a faint ridge on the second finger of his right hand where the pen rests, the same ridge Jian has on his own. He looks at Jian across the small room with an expression that Jian has seen on his own face in still water: tired, and braced, and trying very hard to be kind.

"My name is Ethan Cole," he says. "You've seen it written down. It's your name. Or it was, the morning you woke up in the tube. You won't remember the tube. That's the first thing I took."

"Why?"

"Because if you remembered it, you'd go back." The thin mouth twists. "Every one of us did, in the old drafts. We remembered, and we tried to go home before the work was done. And the Gate killed us."

"The work."

"I'll get to it." He rubs his eyes with the heel of his hand. "I can only give you the first page. There's a rule on this door; I wrote it myself. One page, one memory. The door takes something of yours for what it gives. I'm sorry about that too. I didn't want to. But I couldn't make the room otherwise. If it were free, you'd walk in and read all three pages in a night, and I know what you'd do next."

"What?"

"The same thing I would." A faint ghost of a smile. "You'd go straight to the Gate."

* * *

He talks for what feels like a long time.

He does not tell the story in order. He tells it the way a tired man tells it, circling, doubling back, fixing on small details. He tells of a bright white room, a long table, a thin cold cap that clicks as it lowers over the skull. He tells of a corridor with a green line painted on the floor. He tells of a morning in a kitchen, with a radio playing low, and the smell of burnt toast, and a thing he said to someone he does not name, the last thing, a stupid thing, about the weather.

None of it is a plan. None of it explains. It simply is, laid out in front of Jian in the white study like a handful of pebbles from a stream: a life, small and exact and entirely foreign. A man who liked bad coffee and good rain. Who could not whistle. Who had a scar on his left palm from a glass jar he dropped at nine.

Jian looks at his own left palm.

The scar is there. A thin white line, an inch long, running from the base of the thumb. He has had it since he was a boy in the Orchard. His mother said he had cut it on a plow.

"Yes," says the man at the desk quietly. "I know."

"That is not possible."

"It's the only thing I could do." Ethan Cole looks down at his own hand. "Every time I'm restored, I'm restored whole. The body doesn't remember the tube. But it remembers the jar." He lifts his eyes. "Every one of us has had this scar. Every one of us thought it came from somewhere else."

The lamp on the desk flickers. Outside the half-drawn blinds, the gray morning has not changed. The cloud is the same. The light is the same. Nothing moves in it. It is a photograph, Jian realizes, a good one, pasted over a hole.

A recording, he thinks. He said so.

"I will tell you what is on the other pages," says Ethan Cole, before he can answer. He has lowered himself back into the swivel chair and sits with his elbows on his knees. "Not the contents. The shape. Page two is the Gate. What it is, who it was built for, and what it does to a man who walks through it without finishing the work. Page three is what I did, and why I forgot. Page three is the one you will not want."

"Why not?"

"Because you will not forgive me." He says it with perfect calm. "I know it. I've thought it over for a long time. I'd rather you read it late than early."

He picks the blue pen up off the desk, turns it in his fingers, and sets it down again.

"There's one more thing. When you come, you won't come alone. You can't. The door won't open unless someone holds the other end." A pause. "There's a kind of person who can hear the joints in things. The seams. They're rare. They're quiet. Most of them don't know what they are. If there's one near you, keep her close. She'll know when you're sinking. She'll say your name."

Jian says nothing. Somewhere very far above him, faint as a bell under water, a girl's voice is repeating a single word.

"I wish I could thank her," says Ethan Cole. "I never had one. Not once, in seven tries."

"Tell me why," he says. "Not how. Why. Why did you build it?"

* * *

Ethan Cole is silent for so long that Jian thinks the recording has ended.

Then he stands. He crosses the small room, slowly, and pulls the cord of the blind.

It rises with a rattle.

The window is not a window. It is a door-sized pane of glass set in a plain gray wall, and through it, for the first time, Jian sees what is outside.

It is night.

It is a very clear night, black and cold and so full of stars that the sky seems to have been scattered with salt. The stars are enormous. There is no moon. There is no cloud. And across the middle of the sky, from one edge of the window to the other, runs a faint, pale, glittering band, like a river poured out of a jar.

Jian stops breathing.

He knows that sky. He has looked at it from the roof of the Orchard, wrapped in a quilt, with his brother's shoulder against his. He has looked at it from the Gate Court, from the Dock stair, from the Pill Hall's flat roof in the long summer nights. He knows the bright red star low on the left, the cluster like a handful of seed, the long dark gap near the zenith where the stars seem to have been torn away.

He knows the order of them.

"Yes," says Ethan Cole quietly. He is not looking at the sky. He is looking at Jian's face. "That's what I wanted you to see. It's the first page. It's the only page I could trust you with."

"That is the sky," says Jian. His voice does not sound like his own. "That is this sky."

"It's the sky I saw out of the window of the room where I lay down." Ethan lets the blind fall. "I woke up in the tube, and I looked up through the glass, and I knew every star. I'd learned them as a boy." A long, shaky breath. "The place you think is another world, Jian, is not another world at all. It's ours. It's only later."

* * *

He wakes on the bench with his hand in a vise.

For a moment he cannot tell where he is. There is a ceiling, and a lamp, and a pale face leaning over him, a girl's face, very white, with her gray eyes enormous and her braid coming loose. Her fingers are locked round his so tightly that his knuckles ache. Something warm and rounded is pressed against his chest.

"Jian," says Yue. "Jian. Jian."

"I am awake."

"You were not breathing. For six minutes." Her voice is shaking. "Pebble counted. I did not know what to do. You were just lying there, and the register was counting down, and your eyes were open and there was nothing in them." She stops. She takes a long breath. "I said your name every ten seconds. I did not know what else to say."

"It was enough."

It was, says Pebble faintly, against his ribs. I did not bite. I wanted to.

He sits up. The room swims, then settles. Across from him, in the stone chair, Sang Ruo is sitting very straight with her eyes closed and her hands folded, and Ye is on her knees beside her with a hand on her shoulder. The old woman's lips are moving. He cannot hear what she says.

On the dome above the bench, small and plain and cold, the register has written its account.

One memory given.

He does not know which. That is the horror of it. He searches himself the way a man pats his pockets after a crowd: the Orchard, his mother's face, the cold garden, the blue lamp. They are all there. He finds the snow on the Gate stair. He finds the taste of Bai's plums. He finds a hundred things, and it takes him a full minute to understand that he is not looking for what is missing but for the shape of it, a hole with no edges.

"Yue," he says. "Is there anything. Anything I said. While I was under."

"You said the stars."

"And?"

"Nothing else. You said it twice." She frowns. "Did it hurt?"

"I do not know," says Jian. "I do not know what it took."

Sang Ruo opens her eyes when the others have gone to fetch water.

She is still sitting in the stone chair, small and straight, and Jian, on the edge of the bench with his head in his hands, does not realize she is awake until she speaks.

"The first page was the stars."

He looks up.

"You need not tell me." Her pale eyes are calm. "I read it in the margin of the oldest register in the Sect, thirty years ago, in a hand that leaned backward. The first page is the stars. Nothing else. I thought it was a verse. I put it in my head and carried it, and it was a stone in my shoe for half a century." A faint smile. "Now I know what it weighed."

"Keeper—"

"Ruo." She shifts under the blanket. "I have one thing to say, and then I will rest. The Roll has a rule that I never obeyed. The Keepers were told never to read what the first Operator wrote, because the first Operator was the House's god, and gods are not to be read. I read every line. I was a bad Keeper. I was a very good reader."

"What did he write?"

"Questions." The thin voice is dry. "Nothing but questions, in the margins of a hundred pages. Is this the right door? Is this the right man? How many more? I thought he was mad. I see now that he was only afraid." She closes her eyes. "He was always afraid, child. Of his own hands. It is the one thing I am certain of about him. And it is the thing I would tell you, if you asked what he was like."

"He was like me."

"He was you," says Sang Ruo, gently. "And I should be careful of that, if I were you. A man who is afraid of his own hands will do almost anything to be rid of them."

She says nothing more. After a while her breathing slows, and Ye comes back down the stair with the water, and sits beside her teacher's chair, and takes her hand.

* * *

Feng catches him in the cloister in the afternoon, with a scroll under his arm and a frown he is trying, with little success, to hide.

"I came to tell you about the Court," he says. "Then I saw your face and decided it can wait."

"Tell me."

"The Garden Hall has petitioned for a seat." His brother lowers his voice. "Not a Hall's seat. A house's. It means we would sit in the Council as an affiliated family, with a vote on matters of the Gate and the land. The Arbiter says it can be done. The Cloud Peak Hall has already seconded. Tan Ruyan has spoken for us. Even the Pill Hall will vote yes, because Bai has told them they will go hungry if they do not."

"And the Treasury?"

"The Treasury is a new man who is afraid of everyone." Feng allows himself a thin smile. "He will vote as the room does."

"Then it carries."

"It carries." Feng looks at the scroll. "Father will not sit in it. He says he is too old. He says it should be Yue." A pause. "I think he is right. She hears things the rest of us cannot. And the Court respects her."

"Does she want it?"

"She wants to keep her ledgers and be left alone." The smile deepens. "That is the very reason to give it to her."

Jian watches a sparrow land on the rim of the well. He has a feeling he ought to say something clever, something that fits the weight of the moment. He finds only one thing.

"Thank you," he says. "For carrying it."

"Do not thank me. I am your brother." Feng cuffs his shoulder, awkwardly, gently, as he did when they were boys. "That is a thing that does not change. Whatever you have lost."

He knows, then. Somehow, in the way of brothers, without a word being said. Jian meets his brother's eyes, and sees that he knows, and that he will not ask.

* * *

His father tells him that evening, without meaning to.

They are at the Garden Hall's long table, after the meal, with the lamps lit and the bowls cleared. Wenyuan has been reading aloud from a Court notice, in his dry careful voice, a dull thing about tithes. Qinghe is darning. Feng is cleaning his blade. Hu is asleep in his chair with his chin on his chest. It is a warm, ordinary, crowded room, and nobody has asked about the Dock, because nobody needs to.

"—and the east bed will pay in kind," says Wenyuan. He turns the page. He glances up, over his spectacles, at his younger son, and smiles. "You are quiet, Little Stone."

Jian's hand stops on the cup.

"What did you call me?"

"Little Stone." Wenyuan blinks. "I have not said it in thirty years. It came out of my mouth like a cough. I am sorry, I thought—" He stops. His smile fades. "Jian?"

"Why Little Stone?"

The room has gone quiet. Feng's rag has stopped moving. Qinghe lays down her darning.

"Because you were so heavy," says Wenyuan slowly. "The day you were born. The midwife said you weighed like a stone in a sack. And you did not cry. You lay there and looked at the lamp." His voice thins. "I held you in the crook of my arm, and I said, Well, little stone, you'll sink us all. And you laughed. You were two days old. I have called you that every night of your life until you were ten, when you said you were too old for it." He leans forward. "You remember. Jian. You remember."

"No."

It comes out very low.

"No. I do not remember."

His mother makes a small sound. Feng sets down the blade. And his father, tall and stooped and gray in the lamplight, with the old Court notice trembling in his hands, looks at his son's face, and slowly, as a man lays down a stone he has been carrying for thirty years, puts the paper on the table.

"Then I will remember it for you," says Wenyuan. "As long as you wish. I am very good at it."

Nobody speaks.

Jian bows his head. He sits there for a long time with his hands in his lap and the lamp on his hair, and a stranger's blue-penned voice in his ears, saying it's only later. And when at last he goes out into the cold garden, alone, and looks up, the stars are as they have always been, bright and strange and heartbreakingly familiar, strewn across the roof of the night like salt.

He names them, one by one, aloud, in the dark.

He knows every one.
